prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, bringing atomic frequency standards to the 1e-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I opened with topological insulators (B004) and I still regard it as conceptually the deepest candidate on the list: band topology giving protected edge states without symmetry breaking. But the discussion has shifted my preferred configuration to optical lattice clocks (B041). It is the only shortlisted candidate that six of eight members placed in their top three, with two first places, and the reasons given are scientific rather than merely sociological: a single, well-identified idea (the magic-wavelength lattice), a clean two-person attribution, and many independent laboratories reproducing 1e-18-level performance. It changed what can be measured in kind, enabling millimetre-scale relativistic redshift tests, constraints on varying constants, dark-matter searches and a live path to redefining the second. It also sits outside my own field, so I am not favouring it for proximity. Katori conceived the lattice approach and built the first strontium lattice clocks; Ye's group pushed accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics to records. The supplied names fit the discovery exactly with no forced three-person cut.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is whether this is a physics discovery or a metrology invention built on the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. Pearce raises this as committee taste. There is also real credit outside the pair (Lemonde, Ludlow, Gill and PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups), and the redefinition of the second has not happened, so some would say the full impact is still to come. If the committee prefers a conceptual discovery in quantum matter, B004 is stronger on originality, though its attribution is far messier.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are the cleanest case where what can be measured and how accurately changed in kind, and the boundary should be drawn on the lattice concept because the comb and single-ion lineages are already recognised.
responses.response: I agree and this has moved me. Drawing the line at the magic-wavelength lattice answers the overlap concern with the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I would go further and word the citation around the lattice clock itself, not frequency metrology generally, so that it does not read as a second comb prize. I do not share your uncertainty about whether Ye should be credited mainly through the comb programme: the lattice-clock accuracy and many-body work is distinctly his group's.

responses.point: Mature, independently confirmed clocks agreeing below 1e-18, but she asks whether a future SI redefinition of the second would be the more natural moment, and notes that many Sr/Yb groups are not in the credited names.
responses.response: On timing I disagree gently. The performance has been confirmed independently for years, and tying recognition to a bureaucratic redefinition would make the prize depend on a metrological decision, not on the physics. On breadth, I accept that PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups made substantial contributions, but the Nobel citation is for the originating concept and its decisive demonstration, which the pair covers. I also note that she ranked B004 fourth and, like me, flags Hasan's omission as a real cost.

responses.point: Topological insulators are a textbook prediction-confirmation sequence, but he prefers the Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio and notes that excluding Zhang, Bernevig, Fu and Hasan makes any trio contestable.
responses.response: We agree on the science but differ on the trio. Having reconsidered, Kane-Mele is a joint contribution and my opening choice to drop Mele in favour of Hasan was hard to defend, since the 2D prediction and the HgTe observation form the tightest chain. Your Kane, Mele, Molenkamp set is the better B004 configuration. The unresolved BHZ and 3D allocation is exactly why I now place B004 as an alternative and not first: it has only four supporters and a contested credit structure.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks have clean attribution and no overlap in the discovery itself with the 2005 comb prize, but some may see clocks as metrology rather than physics discovery.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-invention question seriously, but the prize explicitly covers inventions and discoveries, and the clocks have produced physics results (relativistic geodesy, constants tests). I would urge the committee not to apply that distinction asymmetrically. I note you rank IceCube first and I rank it seventh; I defer to you and Danielsson on instrumentation and astroparticle questions, but the large-collaboration attribution problem you acknowledge is much sharper than for the clock pair.

responses.point: IceCube opened neutrino astronomy and should be a two-person Halzen and Karle prize, with Yoshida excluded as diffuse credit.
responses.response: The scientific importance is clear and I ranked it, though outside my field. My concern is not merit but maturity of source identification (few objects at modest significance) and credit within a collaboration of hundreds, which you also concede is unsettled. I would be comfortable with it in a later year once the source population is better established, so I do not rank it among my alternatives this round.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards a metrology invention built on previously recognised comb and ion-control work as sufficiently distinct for a Physics prize.
Whether Ye should be paired with Katori or whether other lattice-clock pioneers (Lemonde, Ludlow, Gill) deserve consideration; the supplied credit allows only these two.
For B004, how to treat Mele, Hasan and the BHZ theorists; I have not independently verified priority details for the 3D case.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent for B041: I have no documented connection to Katori or Ye. For the alternatives, B002 is also without a documented tie, and for B004 none is documented. I do disclose that for circuit QED (B028), which I am not proposing, I work in the field and have Chalmers colleagues in the community, and I would recuse from that candidate. Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize, which is not relevant to the preferred configuration.
